subject: system-design
title: Distributed Logging
summary: Gathering logs from many services into one searchable place through a pipeline of agents, a buffer, and a search backend, so you can reconstruct what happened across a system.

blocks.text: When a system spans dozens of services on hundreds of hosts, the logs that explain a failure are scattered across all of them. Distributed logging collects those streams into one central, searchable place, so debugging a request means running a query instead of SSHing into machines one by one.

items: Low overhead: logging must barely touch a service's latency or CPU.
Little to no loss: logs are most valuable exactly when things are breaking.
Queryable: you must be able to search and filter by time, service, and field.
Scalable: it has to keep up with bursts without falling behind.

blocks.text: Logs flow through three stages. A lightweight agent on each host tails log files and ships lines off-box, keeping the service itself fast. Those lines land in a buffer or queue, often Kafka, that absorbs spikes and decouples producers from storage. From there, logs are written into storage plus a search index, where they can be queried and visualized.

blocks.title: Stitch with a correlation ID
blocks.text: Attach a unique correlation (or trace) ID to each incoming request and pass it to every downstream service. Logging that ID lets you filter on one value and reconstruct the entire path of a single request across services. That is the difference between guessing and seeing.

A single user request may touch ten services, each emitting its own logs. Correlation IDs tie those entries together, and richer tracing adds span IDs so you can see not just which services were involved but the order and timing of each hop. This is what turns a pile of lines into a story you can follow.

At scale, logging everything is too expensive to store and search. Sampling keeps a representative fraction, for instance all errors but only a slice of successful requests, so you keep the signal without drowning in routine traffic. Setting sensible log levels per service is the simplest first lever.

items: Clock skew: each host's clock drifts, so timestamps across machines don't line up perfectly. Ordering events precisely is hard.
Sheer volume: ingest, storage, and index costs grow with the fleet and can dwarf the cost of the services themselves.
Sensitive data: logs easily capture secrets or PII, so scrubbing and access control matter.

blocks.text: The ELK stack is a common embodiment of this pattern, with Kafka frequently buffering in front. It uses Elasticsearch for storage and search, Logstash or lightweight shippers for ingest, and Kibana for visualization.
